name: Đà Lạt Railway Station
summary: An Art Deco railway station from 1938, at the end of a rack railway that once climbed from the coast. Today a short heritage line runs to the village of Trại Mát.

eras.title: Yersin reaches the plateau
eras.text: In June 1893 Alexandre Yersin crossed the Langbiang plateau and found a cool, healthy climate. He recommended it for a mountain resort, and Đà Lạt was built in the following decades.

image.alt: Xuân Hương Lake in Đà Lạt

eras.title: The rack railway
eras.text: A railway from Tháp Chàm on the coast was completed in 1932. On its steepest sections, locomotives used a toothed rack between the rails to climb the mountains.

image.alt: An old train at Đà Lạt station

eras.title: An Art Deco station
eras.text: The new station opened in 1938. Its three pointed roofs are often said to echo the peaks of the Langbiang mountains, and its coloured glass windows light the hall.

eras.label: Early 1970s
eras.title: The line falls silent
eras.text: War damage and attacks forced the mountain railway to stop running. After 1975 much of the track was taken up, and some of the old locomotives were later sold to a heritage railway in Switzerland.

image.alt: Old railway cars at the station

eras.label: 1990s
eras.title: A heritage train
eras.text: A short section of track was reopened for visitors, running about 7 km to the village of Trại Mát and its pagoda decorated with broken porcelain.

image.alt: A railway car at Đà Lạt

eras.label: Today
eras.title: A photo stop
eras.text: The yellow station, its old carriages and steam engine are among the most photographed places in Đà Lạt.

story.title: The doctor who found the plateau
story.narration: Alexandre Yersin was a Swiss-born French doctor, famous for discovering the bacterium that causes plague in 1894. He settled in Nha Trang and loved to explore the mountains. In 1893, travelling with local guides, he reached the high, cool grasslands of Langbiang. He wrote that the plateau would make an ideal sanatorium. The French authorities agreed, and Đà Lạt grew into a resort of villas, lakes and pine forests. Yersin's name is still honoured in the city, on a school, a street and a park.

story.title: Climbing with teeth

image.alt: An old locomotive at Đà Lạt

story.narration: Building a railway from the coast up to 1,500 metres was a huge challenge. Engineers used a rack system on the steepest slopes, near the Krông Pha pass: a toothed rail between the normal rails, gripped by a cog wheel under the locomotive. Swiss-built engines pulled trains up gradients far steeper than a normal railway can handle. In the 1990s, a Swiss heritage railway bought back some of these locomotives and restored them to run in the Alps.

story.title: Giving joy and freshness
story.narration: The name Đà Lạt is thought to come from the K'Ho language: 'đạ' means water or stream, and Lạt is the name of a local people, so it means 'the stream of the Lạt'. The French added a Latin motto whose initials spell the city's name: 'Dat Aliis Laetitiam Aliis Temperiem', 'it gives joy to some, freshness to others'. Whether or not the motto came first, it has stuck, and it still describes the city's appeal.

guide.price: Small entry ticket to the station. A separate ticket for the train to Trại Mát.

hours.notes: Approximate. Heritage trains run several times a day.

do: Ride the heritage train to Trại Mát and visit Linh Phước Pagoda.
Bring a jacket for the cool mornings.
Come early for photos without crowds.
Walk to Xuân Hương Lake, 10 minutes away.
dont: Climb onto the old locomotives where it is not allowed.

tips.title: Đà Lạt food
tips.text: Bánh căn, grilled rice paper (bánh tráng nướng) at the night market, soy milk and artichoke tea.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: Liên Khương airport is 30 km away; buses run from Hồ Chí Minh City (about 7 hours).

tips.title: Nearby
tips.text: Xuân Hương Lake, Đà Lạt market, Bảo Đại's summer palace and the Crazy House.
